questions.question_text: Two blocks ( $P$ and $Q$ ) with respectively masses 2 kg and 1.5 kg are joined by a massless thread. These blocks are mounted on a frictionless pully which is fixed on the edge of a cube $(S)$ , as shown in the figure below. Block $P$ is positioned on the top surface which has no friction and block $Q$ is in contact with side-surface, having coefficient friction $\mu$ . The cube ( $S$ ) moves towards the right with acceleration of $\frac{g}{2}$ , where $g$ is gravitational acceleration. During this movement the block $P$ and $Q$ remain stationary. The value of $\mu$ is $____$ (take $g=10m/s^{2}$ )
questions.question_html: Two blocks ( $P$ and $Q$ ) with respectively masses 2 kg and 1.5 kg are joined by a massless thread. These blocks are mounted on a frictionless pully which is fixed on the edge of a cube $(S)$ , as shown in the figure below. Block $P$ is positioned on the top surface which has no friction and block $Q$ is in contact with side-surface, having coefficient friction $\mu$ . The cube ( $S$ ) moves towards the right with acceleration of $\frac{g}{2}$ , where $g$ is gravitational acceleration. During this movement the block $P$ and $Q$ remain stationary. The value of $\mu$ is $____$ (take $g=10m/s^{2}$ )
questions.explanation_text: Since the cube is accelerating at $a=\frac{g}{2}$ to the right, when analysing the blocks from the cube's non-inertial frame, we must apply a pseudo-force ( $F_{p}=m \times a$ ) on both blocks in the opposite direction to the acceleration of block S. For block P (Mass $m_{P}=2kg$ ) Along horizontal the tension (T) in the thread pulls it to the right. The pseudo-force ( $m_{P} \cdot a$ ) pulls it to the left. Along vertical direction gravity ( $m_{P}g$ ) acts downward and normal force ( $N_{P}$ ) from the top surface acts upward. Since the block is stationary relative to the cube : $T=m_{P} \cdot a=m_{P} \cdot \frac{g}{2}$ $\Rightarrow$ $T=2 \times \frac{10}{2}=10N$ For block Q (Mass $m_{Q}=1.5kg$ ) Along horizontal direction the cube pushes against the block with a normal force $(N_{Q})$ to the right. The pseudoforce $(m_{Q} \cdot a)$ acts to the left. $N_{Q}=m_{Q} \cdot a=1.5 \times \frac{g}{2}$ Along vertical direction, gravity ( $m_{Q}g$ ) acts downward. $F_{gQ}=1.5 \times 10=15N$ Tension (T) in the thread acts upward, $T=10N$ [as the string is massless and inextensible] Friction (f) acts upward to prevent the block from falling. For equilibrium in the vertical direction: $T+f=m_{Q}g$ $\Rightarrow$ $10+f=15 \Rightarrow f=5N$ The friction force is given by $f=\mu N_{Q}$ . $5=\mu \times (1.5 \times \frac{10}{2})$ $\Rightarrow$ $5=\mu \times (1.5 \times 5)$ $\Rightarrow$ $5=\mu \times 7.5$ $\Rightarrow$ $\mu=\frac{5}{7.5}=\frac{2}{3} \approx 0.67$ Therefore, the value of coefficient of friction between the block Q and S is $\mu=0.67$ . Thus, the correct option is (B).

For block P (Mass $m_{P}=2kg$ )

Along horizontal the tension (T) in the thread pulls it to the right. The pseudo-force ( $m_{P} \cdot a$ ) pulls it to the left. Along vertical direction gravity ( $m_{P}g$ ) acts downward and normal force ( $N_{P}$ ) from the top surface acts upward. Since the block is stationary relative to the cube :

$T=m_{P} \cdot a=m_{P} \cdot \frac{g}{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ $T=2 \times \frac{10}{2}=10N$

For block Q (Mass $m_{Q}=1.5kg$ )

Along horizontal direction the cube pushes against the block with a normal force $(N_{Q})$ to the right. The pseudoforce $(m_{Q} \cdot a)$ acts to the left.

$N_{Q}=m_{Q} \cdot a=1.5 \times \frac{g}{2}$

Along vertical direction, gravity ( $m_{Q}g$ ) acts downward.

$F_{gQ}=1.5 \times 10=15N$

Tension (T) in the thread acts upward, $T=10N$ [as the string is massless and inextensible]

Friction (f) acts upward to prevent the block from falling.

For equilibrium in the vertical direction:

$T+f=m_{Q}g$

$\Rightarrow$ $10+f=15 \Rightarrow f=5N$

The friction force is given by $f=\mu N_{Q}$ .

$5=\mu \times (1.5 \times \frac{10}{2})$

$\Rightarrow$ $5=\mu \times (1.5 \times 5)$

$\Rightarrow$ $5=\mu \times 7.5$

$\Rightarrow$ $\mu=\frac{5}{7.5}=\frac{2}{3} \approx 0.67$

Therefore, the value of coefficient of friction between the block Q and S is $\mu=0.67$ .

Thus, the correct option is (B).

questions.question_text: A small block of mass m slides down from the top of a frictionless inclined surface, while the inclined plane is moving towards left with constant acceleration $a_{0}$ . The angle between the inclined plane and ground is $\theta$ and its base length is $L$ . Assuming that initially the small block is at the top of the inclined plane, the time it takes to reach the lowest point of the inclined plane is ________.
questions.question_html: A small block of mass m slides down from the top of a frictionless inclined surface, while the inclined plane is moving towards left with constant acceleration $a_{0}$ . The angle between the inclined plane and ground is $\theta$ and its base length is $L$ . Assuming that initially the small block is at the top of the inclined plane, the time it takes to reach the lowest point of the inclined plane is ________.
questions.explanation_text: The length of the incline (hypotenuse) is given by : $cos\theta=\frac{L}{s} \Rightarrow s=\frac{L}{cos\theta}$ Since the wedge is accelerating to the left with $a_{0}$ , we must work in the non-inertial frame of the wedge. This causes a pseudo-force ( $ma_{0}$ ) acting on the block to the right. We resolve all forces along the surface of the incline : The net acceleration relative to the incline $(a_{rel})$ is : $a_{rel}=\frac{mgsin\theta-ma_{0}cos\theta}{m}=gsin\theta-a_{0}cos\theta$ Using the kinematic equation for distance s starting from rest $(u=0)$ : $s=\frac{1}{2}a_{rel}t^{2}.$ Putting $s=Lcos\theta$ and $a_{\text{rel}}=gsin\theta-a_{0}cos\theta:$ $\frac{L}{cos\theta}=\frac{1}{2}(gsin\theta-a_{0}cos\theta)t^{2}$ $t^{2}=\frac{2L}{cos\theta(gsin\theta-a_{0}cos\theta)}=\frac{2L}{gsin\theta cos\theta-a_{0}cos^{2}\theta}$ Using the identity $2sin\theta cos\theta=sin2\theta$ and $cos^{2}\theta=\frac{1+cos2\theta}{2}$ : $t^{2}=\frac{4L}{2gsin\theta cos\theta-2a_{0}cos^{2}\theta}=\frac{4L}{gsin2\theta-2a_{0}(\frac{1+cos\theta}{2})}$ $\Rightarrow$ $t^{2}=\frac{4L}{gsin2\theta-a_{0}(1+cos\theta)}$ $\Rightarrow t=\sqrt{\frac{4L}{gsin2\theta-a_{0}(1+cos\theta)}}$ Hence, the correct option is (B).
questions.explanation_html:
The length of the incline (hypotenuse) is given by :

$cos\theta=\frac{L}{s} \Rightarrow s=\frac{L}{cos\theta}$

Since the wedge is accelerating to the left with $a_{0}$ , we must work in the non-inertial frame of the wedge. This causes a pseudo-force ( $ma_{0}$ ) acting on the block to the right.

We resolve all forces along the surface of the incline :

The net acceleration relative to the incline $(a_{rel})$ is :

$a_{rel}=\frac{mgsin\theta-ma_{0}cos\theta}{m}=gsin\theta-a_{0}cos\theta$

Using the kinematic equation for distance s starting from rest $(u=0)$ :

$s=\frac{1}{2}a_{rel}t^{2}.$

Putting $s=Lcos\theta$ and $a_{\text{rel}}=gsin\theta-a_{0}cos\theta:$

$\frac{L}{cos\theta}=\frac{1}{2}(gsin\theta-a_{0}cos\theta)t^{2}$

$t^{2}=\frac{2L}{cos\theta(gsin\theta-a_{0}cos\theta)}=\frac{2L}{gsin\theta cos\theta-a_{0}cos^{2}\theta}$

Using the identity $2sin\theta cos\theta=sin2\theta$ and $cos^{2}\theta=\frac{1+cos2\theta}{2}$ :

$t^{2}=\frac{4L}{2gsin\theta cos\theta-2a_{0}cos^{2}\theta}=\frac{4L}{gsin2\theta-2a_{0}(\frac{1+cos\theta}{2})}$

$\Rightarrow$ $t^{2}=\frac{4L}{gsin2\theta-a_{0}(1+cos\theta)}$

$\Rightarrow t=\sqrt{\frac{4L}{gsin2\theta-a_{0}(1+cos\theta)}}$

Hence, the correct option is (B).

questions.question_text: A block is sliding down on an inclined plane of slope $\theta$ and at an instant $t=0$ this block is given an upward momentum so that it starts moving up on the inclined surface with velocity $u$ . The distance $(S)$ travelled by the block before its velocity become zero, is $____$ . (g = gravitational acceleration)
questions.question_html:
A block is sliding down on an inclined plane of slope $\theta$ and at an instant $t=0$ this block is given an upward momentum so that it starts moving up on the inclined surface with velocity $u$ . The distance $(S)$ travelled by the block before its velocity become zero, is $____$ .

(g = gravitational acceleration)
questions.explanation_text: When the block is moving up the inclined plane, the component of gravity acting down the slope opposes its motion. Force along the incline, $F=-mgsin\theta$ Using $F=$ ma, we get $a=-gsin\theta$ . The initial velocity $v_{i}=u$ The final velocity $v_{f}=0$ (since the block comes to rest) Acceleration $a=-gsin\theta$ using the third equation of motion : $v_{f}^{2}=v_{i}^{2}+2aS$ Substitute the values into the equation : $0^{2}=u^{2}+2(-gsin\theta)S$ $\Rightarrow$ $0=u^{2}-2gsin\theta(S)$ $\Rightarrow$ $S=\frac{u^{2}}{2gsin\theta}$ Hence, the distance travelled is $\frac{u^{2}}{2gsin\theta}$ . Hence, correct option is (C).

Force along the incline, $F=-mgsin\theta$

Using $F=$ ma, we get $a=-gsin\theta$ .

The initial velocity $v_{i}=u$

The final velocity $v_{f}=0$ (since the block comes to rest)

Acceleration $a=-gsin\theta$

using the third equation of motion :

$v_{f}^{2}=v_{i}^{2}+2aS$

$0^{2}=u^{2}+2(-gsin\theta)S$

$\Rightarrow$ $0=u^{2}-2gsin\theta(S)$

$\Rightarrow$ $S=\frac{u^{2}}{2gsin\theta}$

Hence, the distance travelled is $\frac{u^{2}}{2gsin\theta}$ . Hence, correct option is (C).

questions.question_text: A block takes $t$ time to slide down a plane inclined at $45^{\circ}$ to the horizontal. If the surface is made smooth (frictionless), the block takes time $\frac{t}{2}$ to slide down the plane. The coefficient of friction between the block and the inclined plane is $(\frac{\alpha}{100})$ . The value of $\alpha$ is $____$ .
questions.question_html: A block takes $t$ time to slide down a plane inclined at $45^{\circ}$ to the horizontal. If the surface is made smooth (frictionless), the block takes time $\frac{t}{2}$ to slide down the plane. The coefficient of friction between the block and the inclined plane is $(\frac{\alpha}{100})$ . The value of $\alpha$ is $____$ .
questions.explanation_text: When a block of mass $m$ is placed on a plane inclined at an angle $\theta$ : Case 1: Rough Surface The forces acting along the plane are the component of gravity ( $mgsin\theta$ ) acting downwards and the kinetic friction ( $f_{k}=\mu N=\mu mgcos\theta$ ) acting upwards. The net force acting along the inclined surface is $F_{\text{net}}=mgsin\theta-\mu mgcos\theta$ Using Newton's second law of motion $F=ma$ , the acceleration of block on rough surface is, $a_{\text{rough}}=g(sin\theta-\mu cos\theta)$ Case 2: Smooth Surface Friction is zero ( $\mu=0$ ). The net force acting along the inclined surface is $F_{\text{net}}=mgsin\theta$ So, the acceleration of block on smooth surface is, $a_{\text{smooth}}=\frac{mgsin\theta}{m}=gsin\theta$ The block starts from rest ( $u=0$ ) and slides a distance s . Using the kinematic equation $s=ut+\frac{1}{2}at^{2}:$ $s=\frac{1}{2}at^{2} \Rightarrow t=\sqrt{\frac{2s}{a}}$ For a constant distance s , the relationship is $t∝\frac{1}{\sqrt{a}}$ , or a $∝\frac{1}{t^{2}}$ . The angle of inclination is $\theta=45^{\circ}$ . The time taken on rough surface is $t_{\text{rough}}=t$ . The time taken on smooth surface is $t_{\text{smooth}}=\frac{t}{2}$ . So, the ratio of accelerations is; $\frac{a_{\text{smooth}}}{a_{\text{rough}}}=(\frac{t_{\text{rough}}}{t_{\text{smooth}}})^{2}=(\frac{t}{t/2})^{2}=(2)^{2}=4$ Substituting the acceleration formulas into the ratio : $\frac{gsin45^{\circ}}{g(sin45^{\circ}-\mu cos45^{\circ})}=4$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{1/\sqrt{2}}{(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}-\mu(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}))}=4$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{1}{1-\mu}=4$ $\Rightarrow$ $1=4-4\mu$ $\Rightarrow$ $4\mu=3 \Rightarrow \mu=0.75=\frac{75}{100}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{75}{100}=\frac{\alpha}{100} \Rightarrow \alpha=75$ Therefore, the value of $\alpha$ is 75 .
questions.explanation_html:
When a block of mass $m$ is placed on a plane inclined at an angle $\theta$ :

Case 1: Rough Surface

The forces acting along the plane are the component of gravity ( $mgsin\theta$ ) acting downwards and the kinetic friction ( $f_{k}=\mu N=\mu mgcos\theta$ ) acting upwards.

The net force acting along the inclined surface is $F_{\text{net}}=mgsin\theta-\mu mgcos\theta$

Using Newton's second law of motion $F=ma$ , the acceleration of block on rough surface is,

$a_{\text{rough}}=g(sin\theta-\mu cos\theta)$

Case 2: Smooth Surface

Friction is zero ( $\mu=0$ ).

The net force acting along the inclined surface is $F_{\text{net}}=mgsin\theta$

So, the acceleration of block on smooth surface is,

$a_{\text{smooth}}=\frac{mgsin\theta}{m}=gsin\theta$

The block starts from rest ( $u=0$ ) and slides a distance s .

Using the kinematic equation $s=ut+\frac{1}{2}at^{2}:$

$s=\frac{1}{2}at^{2} \Rightarrow t=\sqrt{\frac{2s}{a}}$

For a constant distance s , the relationship is $t∝\frac{1}{\sqrt{a}}$ , or a $∝\frac{1}{t^{2}}$ .

The angle of inclination is $\theta=45^{\circ}$ .

The time taken on rough surface is $t_{\text{rough}}=t$ .

The time taken on smooth surface is $t_{\text{smooth}}=\frac{t}{2}$ .

So, the ratio of accelerations is;

$\frac{a_{\text{smooth}}}{a_{\text{rough}}}=(\frac{t_{\text{rough}}}{t_{\text{smooth}}})^{2}=(\frac{t}{t/2})^{2}=(2)^{2}=4$

Substituting the acceleration formulas into the ratio :

$\frac{gsin45^{\circ}}{g(sin45^{\circ}-\mu cos45^{\circ})}=4$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{1/\sqrt{2}}{(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}-\mu(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}))}=4$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{1}{1-\mu}=4$

$\Rightarrow$ $1=4-4\mu$

$\Rightarrow$ $4\mu=3 \Rightarrow \mu=0.75=\frac{75}{100}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{75}{100}=\frac{\alpha}{100} \Rightarrow \alpha=75$

Therefore, the value of $\alpha$ is 75 .

questions.question_text: Three masses $m_{1}=4kg,m_{2}=4kg$ and $m_{3}=6kg$ are suspended from a fixed smooth frictionless pully as shown in the figure below. The value of $T_{1}/T_{2}$ is $____$ (take $g=10m/s^{2}$ )
questions.question_html:
Three masses $m_{1}=4kg,m_{2}=4kg$ and $m_{3}=6kg$ are suspended from a fixed smooth frictionless pully as shown in the figure below. The value of $T_{1}/T_{2}$ is

$____$

(take $g=10m/s^{2}$ )
questions.explanation_text: The masses $m_{1}$ and $m_{2}$ are on one side of the pulley, and $m_{3}$ is on the other. Total mass on right side is $M_{R}=m_{2}+m_{3}=4+6=10kg$ . Total mass on right side is $M_{L}=m_{1}=4kg$ . Since $M_{L}<M_{R}$ , the system will accelerate toward the right side. Let the acceleration be $a$ . For right side, $m_{R}g-T_{1}=m_{R}a \Rightarrow 10g-T_{1}=10a$ For left side, $T_{1}-m_{L}g=m_{L}a \Rightarrow T_{1}-4g=4a\dots$ From both the equations, $T_{1}-4g=4(\frac{10g-T_{1}}{10}) \Rightarrow \frac{10}{4}(T_{1}-40)=100-T_{1}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{5T_{1}}{2}-100=100-T_{1} \Rightarrow \frac{5T_{1}}{2}+T_{1}=200$ $\Rightarrow \frac{7T_{1}}{2}=200 \Rightarrow T_{1}=\frac{400}{7}N\dots(ii)$ Putting in equation (ii), we get the acceleration of the system; $a=\frac{T_{1}-4g}{4}=\frac{\frac{400}{7}-40}{4}=\frac{120}{7 \times 4}=\frac{30}{7}m/s^{2}\dots(iv)$ The acceleration of whole system is $30/7m/s^{2}$ , For mass $m_{3}$ ; $m_{3}g-T_{2}=m_{3}a \Rightarrow T_{2}=m_{3}(g-a)$ $T_{2}=6(10-\frac{30}{7})N=6 \times \frac{40}{7}=\frac{240}{7}\dots(v)$ So, the ratio is $\frac{T_{1}}{T_{2}}$ is; $\frac{T_{1}}{T_{2}}=\frac{400/7}{240/7}=\frac{400}{240}=\frac{5}{3}$ Therefore, the correct option is (A).
questions.explanation_html:
The masses $m_{1}$ and $m_{2}$ are on one side of the pulley, and $m_{3}$ is on the other.

Total mass on right side is $M_{R}=m_{2}+m_{3}=4+6=10kg$ .

Total mass on right side is $M_{L}=m_{1}=4kg$ .

Since $M_{L}<M_{R}$ , the system will accelerate toward the right side. Let the acceleration be $a$ .

For right side, $m_{R}g-T_{1}=m_{R}a \Rightarrow 10g-T_{1}=10a$

For left side, $T_{1}-m_{L}g=m_{L}a \Rightarrow T_{1}-4g=4a\dots$

From both the equations,

$T_{1}-4g=4(\frac{10g-T_{1}}{10}) \Rightarrow \frac{10}{4}(T_{1}-40)=100-T_{1}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{5T_{1}}{2}-100=100-T_{1} \Rightarrow \frac{5T_{1}}{2}+T_{1}=200$

$\Rightarrow \frac{7T_{1}}{2}=200 \Rightarrow T_{1}=\frac{400}{7}N\dots(ii)$

Putting in equation (ii), we get the acceleration of the system;

$a=\frac{T_{1}-4g}{4}=\frac{\frac{400}{7}-40}{4}=\frac{120}{7 \times 4}=\frac{30}{7}m/s^{2}\dots(iv)$

The acceleration of whole system is $30/7m/s^{2}$ ,

For mass $m_{3}$ ;

$m_{3}g-T_{2}=m_{3}a \Rightarrow T_{2}=m_{3}(g-a)$

$T_{2}=6(10-\frac{30}{7})N=6 \times \frac{40}{7}=\frac{240}{7}\dots(v)$

So, the ratio is $\frac{T_{1}}{T_{2}}$ is;

$\frac{T_{1}}{T_{2}}=\frac{400/7}{240/7}=\frac{400}{240}=\frac{5}{3}$

Therefore, the correct option is (A).

questions.question_text: A block of mass 5 kg is moving on an inclined plane which makes an angle of $30^{\circ}$ with the horizontal. Friction coefficient between the block and inclined plane surface is $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ . The force to be applied on the block so that the block will move down without acceleration is $____$ N. $(g=10m/s^{2}).$
questions.question_html:
A block of mass 5 kg is moving on an inclined plane which makes an angle of $30^{\circ}$ with the horizontal. Friction coefficient between the block and inclined plane surface is $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ . The force to be applied on the block so that the block will move down without acceleration is $____$ N.

$(g=10m/s^{2}).$
questions.explanation_text: The forces acting on the block are, Component of weight down the plane (along x -axis) $=mgsin\theta=5 \times 10 \times sin30^{\circ}=25N$ Normal Force, $N=mgcos\theta$ Since the block moves down, friction acts up the plane. $f_{k}=\mu_{k}N=\mu(mgcos\theta)$ Maximum frictional force : $f_{k}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \times (5 \times 10 \times cos(30^{\circ}))$ $\Rightarrow$ $f_{k}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \times (50 \times \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})=\frac{3}{4} \times 50=37.5N$ Since the upward frictional force ( 37.5 N ) is greater than the downward component of weight ( 25 N ), the block will not move down on its own. To make it move down at a constant velocity, an additional downward force (P) must be applied. The equilibrium equation along the incline is : Net Force Downward $=$ Net Force Upward $P+F_{\text{weight}}=f_{k}$ $\Rightarrow$ $P+25=37.5$ $P=37.5-25=12.5N$ Hence, the correct option is (B).
questions.explanation_html:
The forces acting on the block are,

Component of weight down the plane (along x -axis) $=mgsin\theta=5 \times 10 \times sin30^{\circ}=25N$

Normal Force, $N=mgcos\theta$

Since the block moves down, friction acts up the plane.

$f_{k}=\mu_{k}N=\mu(mgcos\theta)$

Maximum frictional force :

$f_{k}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \times (5 \times 10 \times cos(30^{\circ}))$

$\Rightarrow$ $f_{k}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \times (50 \times \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})=\frac{3}{4} \times 50=37.5N$

Since the upward frictional force ( 37.5 N ) is greater than the downward component of weight ( 25 N ), the block will not move down on its own. To make it move down at a constant velocity, an additional downward force (P) must be applied.

The equilibrium equation along the incline is :

Net Force Downward $=$ Net Force Upward

$P+F_{\text{weight}}=f_{k}$

$\Rightarrow$ $P+25=37.5$

$P=37.5-25=12.5N$

Hence, the correct option is (B).

questions.question_text: A 4 kg mass moves under the influence of a force $\vec{F}=(4t^{3}\hat{i}-3t\hat{j})N$ where $t$ is the time in second. If mass starts from origin at $t=0$ , the velocity and position after $t=2s$ will be:
questions.question_html: A 4 kg mass moves under the influence of a force $\vec{F}=(4t^{3}\hat{i}-3t\hat{j})N$ where $t$ is the time in second. If mass starts from origin at $t=0$ , the velocity and position after $t=2s$ will be:
questions.explanation_text: According to Newton's Second Law $\vec{F}=m\vec{a}$ . $\vec{a}=\frac{\vec{F}}{m}$ Given $m=4kg$ and $\vec{F}=4t^{3}\hat{ı}-3t\hat{ȷ}$ : $\vec{a}=\frac{4t^{3}\hat{ı}-3t\hat{ȷ}}{4}=(t^{3}\hat{ı}-\frac{3}{4}t\hat{ȷ})m/s^{2}$ Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity : $\vec{a}=\frac{d\vec{v}}{dt}$ Since the mass starts from rest at the origin at $t=0$ , we have $\vec{v}(0)=0$ $\int_{0}^{\vec{v}}d\vec{v}=\int_{0}^{t}(t^{3}\hat{ı}-\frac{3}{4}t\hat{ȷ})dt$ $\Rightarrow$ $\vec{v}=(\frac{t^{4}}{4}\hat{ı}-\frac{3t^{2}}{8}\hat{ȷ})m/s$ So, velocity at $t=2s$ is : $\vec{v}=\frac{2^{4}}{4}\hat{ı}-\frac{3(2^{2})}{8}\hat{ȷ}=\frac{16}{4}\hat{ı}-\frac{12}{8}\hat{ȷ}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\vec{v}=(4\hat{ı}-\frac{3}{2}\hat{ȷ})m/s$ Velocity is the rate of change of position : $\vec{v}=\frac{d\vec{r}}{dt} \Rightarrow d\vec{r}=\vec{v}dt$ At $t=0$ , the mass is at the origin ( $\vec{r}=0$ ), $\int_{0}^{\vec{r}}d\vec{r}=\int_{0}^{t}(\frac{t^{4}}{4}\hat{ı}-\frac{3t^{2}}{8}\hat{ȷ})dt$ $\Rightarrow$ $\vec{r}=(\frac{t^{5}}{20}\hat{ı}-\frac{t^{3}}{8}\hat{ȷ})_{0}^{t}m$ $\Rightarrow$ $\vec{r}=[\frac{t^{5}}{20}\hat{ı}-\frac{t^{3}}{8}\hat{ȷ}]-[\frac{0^{5}}{20}\hat{ı}-\frac{0^{3}}{8}\hat{ȷ}]m$ $\Rightarrow$ $\vec{r}=(\frac{t^{5}}{20}\hat{ı}-\frac{t^{3}}{8}\hat{ȷ})$ Now, calculate position at $t=2s$ : $\vec{r}=\frac{2^{5}}{20}\hat{ı}-\frac{2^{3}}{8}\hat{ȷ}=\frac{32}{20}\hat{ı}-\frac{8}{8}\hat{ȷ}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\vec{r}=\frac{8}{5}\hat{ı}-1\hat{ȷ}=(\frac{8}{5}\hat{ı}-\hat{ȷ})m$ Therefore, at $t=2s$ , the velocity is $\vec{v}=4\hat{ı}-\frac{3}{2}\hat{ȷ}$ and the position vector is $\vec{r}=\frac{8}{5}\hat{ı}-\hat{ȷ}$ . Hence, the correct option is (C).
questions.explanation_html:
According to Newton's Second Law $\vec{F}=m\vec{a}$ .

$\vec{a}=\frac{\vec{F}}{m}$

Given $m=4kg$ and $\vec{F}=4t^{3}\hat{ı}-3t\hat{ȷ}$ :

$\vec{a}=\frac{4t^{3}\hat{ı}-3t\hat{ȷ}}{4}=(t^{3}\hat{ı}-\frac{3}{4}t\hat{ȷ})m/s^{2}$

Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity :

$\vec{a}=\frac{d\vec{v}}{dt}$

Since the mass starts from rest at the origin at $t=0$ , we have $\vec{v}(0)=0$

$\int_{0}^{\vec{v}}d\vec{v}=\int_{0}^{t}(t^{3}\hat{ı}-\frac{3}{4}t\hat{ȷ})dt$

$\Rightarrow$ $\vec{v}=(\frac{t^{4}}{4}\hat{ı}-\frac{3t^{2}}{8}\hat{ȷ})m/s$

So, velocity at $t=2s$ is :

$\vec{v}=\frac{2^{4}}{4}\hat{ı}-\frac{3(2^{2})}{8}\hat{ȷ}=\frac{16}{4}\hat{ı}-\frac{12}{8}\hat{ȷ}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\vec{v}=(4\hat{ı}-\frac{3}{2}\hat{ȷ})m/s$

Velocity is the rate of change of position :

$\vec{v}=\frac{d\vec{r}}{dt} \Rightarrow d\vec{r}=\vec{v}dt$

At $t=0$ , the mass is at the origin ( $\vec{r}=0$ ),

questions.explanation_text: As the particle falls, two forces act on it : Weight $(F_{g}=mg)$ acting downwards. Resistive Force ( $F=kv$ ) acting upwards (opposing motion). The net force on the particle is, $F_{net}=mg-kv$ According to Newton's Second Law, $F_{net}=m \cdot a=m\frac{dv}{dt}$ . Therefore $m\frac{dv}{dt}=mg-kv$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{dv}{mg-kv}=\frac{1}{m}dt$ Integrate both sides, knowing that at $t=0,v=0$ (starting from rest) : $\int_{0}^{v}\frac{dv}{mg-kv}=\frac{1}{m}\int_{0}^{t}dt$ $\Rightarrow$ $-\frac{1}{k}[ln(mg-kv)]_{0}^{v}=\frac{t}{m}$ $\Rightarrow$ $ln(\frac{mg-kv}{mg})=-\frac{k}{m}t$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{mg-kv}{mg}=e^{-\frac{k}{m}t}$ $\Rightarrow$ $1-\frac{kv}{mg}=e^{-\frac{k}{m}t}$ $\Rightarrow$ $v(t)=\frac{mg}{k}(1-e^{-\frac{k}{m}t})$ The resulting equation $v(t)=v_{t}(1-e^{-\frac{t}{\tau}})$ where $v_{t}=\frac{mg}{k}$ is the terminal velocity. At $t=0,v=v_{t}(1-1)=0$ . Hence, the graph must start at the origin $(0,0)$ . As $t \rightarrow \infty$ the term $e^{-\frac{k}{m}t}$ approaches 0 , so v approaches a constant value $\frac{mg}{k}$ (terminal velocity). This is an exponential graph with a horizontal asymptote at $v=\frac{mg}{k}$ Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.question_html: The time taken by a block of mass $m$ to slide down from the highest point to the lowest point on a rough inclined plane is $50%$ more compared to the time taken by the same block on identical inclined smooth plane. Both inclined planes are at $45^{\circ}$ with the horizontal. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the rough inclined surface and block is $____$
questions.explanation_text: For smooth inclined plane : When the plane is smooth, there is no friction. The only forces acting on the block along the incline are the component of gravity ( $mgsin\theta$ ). According to Newton's Second Law : $F_{net}=ma$ $\Rightarrow$ $mgsin\theta=ma_{s}$ $\Rightarrow$ $a_{s}=gsin\theta$ Using the second equation of motion, $S=ut+\frac{1}{2}at^{2}$ , where the block starts from rest $(u=0)$ and travels a distance L (length of the incline): $L=\frac{1}{2}a_{s}t_{s}^{2}$ $\Rightarrow$ $t_{s}=\sqrt{\frac{2L}{a_{s}}}=\sqrt{\frac{2L}{gsin\theta}}$ For rough inclined plane : On a rough plane, kinetic friction ( $f_{k}$ ) acts upwards against the motion. The normal force is $N=mgcos\theta$ , so $f_{k}=\mu_{k}N=\mu_{k}mgcos\theta$ . The net force along the incline is : $F_{net}=mgsin\theta-\mu_{k}mgcos\theta$ $\Rightarrow$ $ma_{r}=m(gsin\theta-\mu_{k}gcos\theta)$ $\Rightarrow$ $a_{r}=g(sin\theta-\mu_{k}cos\theta)$ The time taken $t_{r}$ to travel the same distance L is: $t_{r}=\sqrt{\frac{2L}{a_{r}}}=\sqrt{\frac{2L}{g(sin\theta-\mu_{k}cos\theta)}}$ It is given that $t_{r}$ is $50%$ more than $t_{s}$ . $t_{r}=t_{s}+0.5t_{s}=1.5t_{s}=\frac{3}{2}t_{s}$ $\Rightarrow$ $t_{r}^{2}=\frac{9}{4}t_{s}^{2}$ Substituting the expressions for $t_{r}^{2}$ and $t_{s}^{2}$ : $\frac{2L}{g(sin\theta-\mu_{k}cos\theta)}=\frac{9}{4}(\frac{2L}{gsin\theta})$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{1}{sin\theta-\mu_{k}cos\theta}=\frac{9}{4sin\theta}$ $\Rightarrow$ $4sin\theta=9sin\theta-9\mu_{k}cos\theta$ $\Rightarrow$ $9\mu_{k}cos\theta=5sin\theta$ $\Rightarrow$ $\mu_{k}=\frac{5}{9}tan\theta$ The angle of inclination is $\theta=45^{\circ}$ $\mu_{k}=\frac{5}{9}tan45^{\circ}=\frac{5}{9}$ Therefore, the correct option is (C).
questions.explanation_html:
For smooth inclined plane :

When the plane is smooth, there is no friction. The only forces acting on the block along the incline are the component of gravity ( $mgsin\theta$ ).

According to Newton's Second Law :

$F_{net}=ma$

$\Rightarrow$ $mgsin\theta=ma_{s}$

$\Rightarrow$ $a_{s}=gsin\theta$

Using the second equation of motion, $S=ut+\frac{1}{2}at^{2}$ , where the block starts from rest $(u=0)$ and travels a distance L (length of the incline):

$L=\frac{1}{2}a_{s}t_{s}^{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ $t_{s}=\sqrt{\frac{2L}{a_{s}}}=\sqrt{\frac{2L}{gsin\theta}}$

For rough inclined plane :

On a rough plane, kinetic friction ( $f_{k}$ ) acts upwards against the motion.

The normal force is $N=mgcos\theta$ , so $f_{k}=\mu_{k}N=\mu_{k}mgcos\theta$ .

The net force along the incline is :

$F_{net}=mgsin\theta-\mu_{k}mgcos\theta$

$\Rightarrow$ $ma_{r}=m(gsin\theta-\mu_{k}gcos\theta)$

$\Rightarrow$ $a_{r}=g(sin\theta-\mu_{k}cos\theta)$

The time taken $t_{r}$ to travel the same distance L is:

$t_{r}=\sqrt{\frac{2L}{a_{r}}}=\sqrt{\frac{2L}{g(sin\theta-\mu_{k}cos\theta)}}$

It is given that $t_{r}$ is $50%$ more than $t_{s}$ .

$t_{r}=t_{s}+0.5t_{s}=1.5t_{s}=\frac{3}{2}t_{s}$

$\Rightarrow$ $t_{r}^{2}=\frac{9}{4}t_{s}^{2}$

Substituting the expressions for $t_{r}^{2}$ and $t_{s}^{2}$ :

$\frac{2L}{g(sin\theta-\mu_{k}cos\theta)}=\frac{9}{4}(\frac{2L}{gsin\theta})$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{1}{sin\theta-\mu_{k}cos\theta}=\frac{9}{4sin\theta}$

$\Rightarrow$ $4sin\theta=9sin\theta-9\mu_{k}cos\theta$

$\Rightarrow$ $9\mu_{k}cos\theta=5sin\theta$

$\Rightarrow$ $\mu_{k}=\frac{5}{9}tan\theta$

The angle of inclination is $\theta=45^{\circ}$

$\mu_{k}=\frac{5}{9}tan45^{\circ}=\frac{5}{9}$

Therefore, the correct option is (C).

Given:

The equation of the surface: $y=\frac{x^{2}}{4}$ .

Coefficient of friction: $\mu=0.5$ .

Gravitational acceleration: $g$ (assumed constant).

1. Slope of the Surface:

The slope of the surface at any point is given by:

$tan\theta=\frac{dy}{dx}$

From the equation of the surface:

$y=\frac{x^{2}}{4}$

Differentiating with respect to $x$ :

$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{x}{2}$

Thus, the slope at any point is:

$tan\theta=\frac{x}{2}$

2. Forces Acting on the Block:

At the point where the block is placed:

Weight of the block acts vertically downward: $mg$ .

Normal force acts perpendicular to the surface.

Frictional force acts parallel to the surface, opposing the component of the weight that causes slipping.

3. Condition for No Slipping:

The block will not slip if the frictional force is sufficient to counteract the component of the gravitational force parallel to the slope. The frictional force is:

$f=\mu N$

The normal force $N$ is given by:

$N=mgcos\theta$

The component of weight parallel to the slope is:

$F_{\text{parallel}}=mgsin\theta$

For the block to not slip:

$f \ge F_{\text{parallel}}$

Substitute $f=\mu N$ and $N=mgcos\theta$ :

$\mu(mgcos\theta) \ge mgsin\theta$

Simplify:

$\mu cos\theta \ge sin\theta$

Divide through by $cos\theta$ :

questions.explanation_text: To find the angle between $\vec{F}$ and $\vec{p}$ , we first need to understand the relationship between force and momentum. The force $\vec{F}$ acting on a particle is related to the rate of change of its linear momentum $\vec{p}$ with respect to time, as described by Newton's second law of motion: $\vec{F}=\frac{d\vec{p}}{dt}$ Given the expression for the momentum $\vec{p}(t)=\hat{i}cos(kt)-\hat{j}sin(kt)$ , we can find $\vec{F}$ by differentiating $\vec{p}$ with respect to $t$ : $\frac{d\vec{p}}{dt}=-k\hat{i}sin(kt)-k\hat{j}cos(kt)$ So, $\vec{F}=-k\hat{i}sin(kt)-k\hat{j}cos(kt)$ . Now, to find the angle between $\vec{F}$ and $\vec{p}$ , we use the dot product formula: $\vec{F} \cdot \vec{p}=|\vec{F}||\vec{p}|cos(\theta)$ , where $\theta$ is the angle between $\vec{F}$ and $\vec{p}$ . However, in this case, it's more insightful to see if $\vec{F}$ and $\vec{p}$ are orthogonal (at a $\frac{\pi}{2}$ angle to each other), because the dot product of two perpendicular vectors is zero. The dot product of $\vec{F}$ and $\vec{p}$ is: $(-k\hat{i}sin(kt)-k\hat{j}cos(kt)) \cdot (\hat{i}cos(kt)-\hat{j}sin(kt))=$ $-ksin(kt)cos(kt)+kcos(kt)sin(kt)=0$ The result is zero, indicating that the angle between $\vec{F}$ and $\vec{p}$ is indeed $\frac{\pi}{2}$ . Therefore, the correct option is: Option A $\frac{\pi}{2}$ .

questions.question_html: A cricket player catches a ball of mass $120g$ moving with $25m/s$ speed. If the catching process is completed in $0.1s$ then the magnitude of force exerted by the ball on the hand of player will be (in SI unit) :
questions.explanation_text: The first step in solving this problem is to calculate the change in momentum of the ball when it is caught. The change in momentum, or impulse, is the product of the mass of the ball and the change in velocity (as momentum is mass times velocity). The ball is initially moving with a velocity of $v_{i}=25m/s$ before the catch and finally comes to rest with a velocity of $v_{f}=0m/s$ after the catch. Since the ball is caught, the final velocity is zero. The change in velocity $\Delta v=v_{f}-v_{i}=0-25=-25m/s.$ Remember that the direction of the force exerted by the ball on the hand will be opposite to the direction of the ball's initial motion. The mass of the ball $m$ is given as $120g$ which needs to be converted into kilograms to maintain SI units: $m=120g=120 \times 10^{-3}kg=0.12kg.$ Now we can calculate the change in momentum (impulse): $\Delta p=m\Delta v=0.12kg \times (-25m/s).$ Substituting the values we get: $\Delta p=0.12 \times -25=-3kg \cdot m/s.$ The negative sign indicates that the change in momentum is in the opposite direction of the ball's initial motion, which makes sense because the ball's velocity is reduced to zero. The magnitude of the impulse is independent of the sign and is $3kg \cdot m/s$ . Impulse is also equal to the average force exerted on the ball times the time interval during which the force is exerted. We can use the formula: $\Delta p=F_{avg}\Delta t$ Where $F_{avg}$ is the average force and $\Delta t$ is the time interval of $0.1s$ . Re-arranging the formula to solve for $F_{avg}$ gives us: $F_{avg}=\frac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}.$ Substituting the known values we have: $F_{avg}=\frac{3}{0.1}=30N.$ The magnitude of the average force exerted by the hand of the player to catch the ball is $30N$ .

questions.explanation_text: Let's analyze both statements: Statement (I): The limiting force of static friction depends on the area of contact and independent of materials. This statement is incorrect. The limiting force of static friction does not depend on the area of contact but is dependent on the materials in contact. According to the law of static friction, the maximum static frictional force $f_{s}$ that can occur before motion commences is given by the product of the coefficient of static friction $\mu_{s}$ and the normal reaction force $N$ : $f_{s}=\mu_{s} \times N$ The coefficient $\mu_{s}$ is a property that depends on the materials in contact, not on the area of contact. The normal force $N$ is the force perpendicular to the surfaces in contact, influenced by the weight of the object and any other perpendicular forces acting upon it. Statement (II): The limiting force of kinetic friction is independent of the area of contact and depends on materials. This statement is correct. Once an object is in motion, the kinetic frictional force $f_{k}$ opposing its motion is given by the product of the coefficient of kinetic friction $\mu_{k}$ and the normal force $N$ : $f_{k}=\mu_{k} \times N$ The coefficient $\mu_{k}$ , like $\mu_{s}$ , is also a property dependent on the materials of the surfaces in contact. It generally has a lower value than $\mu_{s}$ , which is why objects tend to be easier to keep moving once they've started. The kinetic frictional force is independent of the area of contact between the two surfaces. Given these explanations, the correct answer would be: Option A : Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

questions.explanation_text: Let's denote the magnitude of the smaller force as $F$ , hence the magnitude of the larger force is $3F$ . The resultant force $\vec{R}$ is equal in magnitude to the larger force, which means $|\vec{R}|=3F$ . When two forces $\vec{F}_{1}$ and $\vec{F}_{2}$ act on a body, the magnitude of their resultant $\vec{R}$ can be found using the law of vector addition: $|\vec{R}|=\sqrt{|\vec{F}_{1}|^{2}+|\vec{F}_{2}|^{2}+2|\vec{F}_{1}||\vec{F}_{2}|cos\theta}$ , where $\theta$ is the angle between $\vec{F}_{1}$ and $\vec{F}_{2}$ . Given that in our case $|\vec{R}|=3F$ , $|\vec{F}_{1}|=F$ and $|\vec{F}_{2}|=3F$ , by substituting these values into the equation, we get: $3F=\sqrt{F^{2}+(3F)^{2}+2(F)(3F)cos\theta}$ $9F^{2}=F^{2}+9F^{2}+6F^{2}cos\theta$ Simplifying this equation by subtracting $10F^{2}$ from both sides gives: $-F^{2}=6F^{2}cos\theta$ Dividing both sides by $-F^{2}$ gives: $-1=-6cos\theta$ Therefore, $cos\theta=\frac{1}{6}$ . It is given that the angle between $\vec{F}_{1}$ and $\vec{F}_{2}$ is $cos^{-1}(\frac{1}{n})$ , hence comparing this with the above result, we find that $n=6$ . Therefore, $|n|=6$ .

Given that $F_{2}$ and $F_{3}$ are acting perpendicularly, we can represent the balance of forces as follows: $F_{1}=\sqrt{F_{2}^{2}+F_{3}^{2}}$ We can now calculate the equivalent force resulting from $F_{2}$ and $F_{3}$ : $F_{1}=\sqrt{(8N)^{2}+(6N)^{2}}=\sqrt{64+36}=\sqrt{100}=10N$ Since the particle is initially at rest, when the force $F_{1}$ is removed, only $F_{2}$ and $F_{3}$ remain. The net force acting on the particle is the equivalent force resulting from $F_{2}$ and $F_{3}$ , which we have calculated to be $10N$ . Now, we can use Newton's second law to find the acceleration of the particle: $F=ma$ Where: $F$ is the net force acting on the particle $m$ is the mass of the particle $a$ is the acceleration of the particle Rearranging the equation to solve for $a$ : $a=\frac{F}{m}$ Plugging in the values for $F$ and $m$ : $a=\frac{10N}{5kg}=2ms^{-2}$ The acceleration of the particle when the force $F_{1}$ is removed is $2ms^{-2}$ , which corresponds to Option C.

questions.explanation_text:
Given that the velocity of the body varies with displacement x according to the relation: $v=10\sqrt{x}ms^{-1}$ To find the force acting on the body, we first need to find its acceleration, which can be obtained by differentiating the velocity with respect to time. However, we don't have the velocity expressed as a function of time, but rather as a function of displacement. To work around this, we will use the chain rule: $\frac{dv}{dt}=\frac{dv}{dx} \cdot \frac{dx}{dt}$ Now, differentiate the velocity with respect to displacement: $\frac{dv}{dx}=\frac{1}{2} \cdot 10 \cdot x^{-1/2}=5x^{-1/2}$ Recall that $\frac{dx}{dt}$ is the velocity, so we have: $\frac{dv}{dt}=5x^{-1/2} \cdot 10\sqrt{x}=50$ Thus, the acceleration is constant and equal to 50 m/s².

Now we can find the force acting on the body using Newton's second law: $F=ma$ First, convert the mass from grams to kilograms: $m=\frac{500g}{1000}=0.5kg$ Now, calculate the force: $F=(0.5kg)(50ms^{-2})=25N$ The force acting on the body is 25 N.

questions.question_text: A person standing on a spring balance inside a stationary lift measures 60 kg. The weight of that person if the lift descends with uniform downward acceleration of 1.8 m/s 2 will be ______________ N. [g = 10 m/s 2 ]
questions.question_html: A person standing on a spring balance inside a stationary lift measures 60 kg. The weight of that person if the lift descends with uniform downward acceleration of 1.8 m/s2 will be ______________ N. [g = 10 m/s2]
questions.explanation_text: The apparent weight $W_{\text{app}}$ of a person in an elevator moving with acceleration is given by: $W_{\text{app}}=m(g-a)$ where: $W_{\text{app}}$ is the apparent weight, $m$ is the mass of the person, $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity, $a$ is the acceleration of the elevator. Given that the person's mass is 60 kg, the acceleration due to gravity is 10 m/s², and the acceleration of the lift is 1.8 m/s², we can substitute these values into the formula: $W_{\text{app}}=60\text{kg} \times (10\text{m/s}^{2}-1.8\text{m/s}^{2})=60\text{kg} \times 8.2\text{m/s}^{2}=492\text{N}$ So, the apparent weight of the person when the lift descends with a uniform downward acceleration of 1.8 m/s² will be 492 N.
questions.explanation_html:
The apparent weight $W_{\text{app}}$ of a person in an elevator moving with acceleration is given by:

$W_{\text{app}}=m(g-a)$

where:

  • $W_{\text{app}}$ is the apparent weight,
  • $m$ is the mass of the person,
  • $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity,
  • $a$ is the acceleration of the elevator.

Given that the person's mass is 60 kg, the acceleration due to gravity is 10 m/s², and the acceleration of the lift is 1.8 m/s², we can substitute these values into the formula:

$W_{\text{app}}=60\text{kg} \times (10\text{m/s}^{2}-1.8\text{m/s}^{2})=60\text{kg} \times 8.2\text{m/s}^{2}=492\text{N}$

So, the apparent weight of the person when the lift descends with a uniform downward acceleration of 1.8 m/s² will be 492 N.

questions.question_html: A ball is thrown upward with an initial velocity V0 from the surface of the earth. The motion of the ball is affected by a drag force equal to m $\gamma$ u2 (where m is mass of the ball, u is its instantaneous velocity and $\gamma$ is a constant). Time taken by the ball to rise to its zenith is :
questions.explanation_text: Given, drag force, $F=m\gamma v^{2}$ ......(i) As we know, general equation of force $=ma$ .........(ii) Comparing Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get $a=\gamma v^{2}$ The net retardation of the ball when thrown vertically upward is therefore $a_{\text{net}}=-(g+\gamma v^{2})=\frac{dv}{dt}$ , where $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity. Rearranging terms gives us : $\frac{dv}{g+\gamma v^{2}}=-dt$ We now need to integrate both sides of this equation. When the ball is thrown upward with velocity $v_{0}$ and reaches its zenith ( "zenith" refers to the highest point that the ball reaches in its upward trajectory.), the velocity is $0$ . The time to reach the zenith is $t$ . So the integral equation is : $\int_{v_{0}}^{0}\frac{dv}{\gamma v^{2}+g}=-\int_{0}^{t}dt$ Separating the constants from the integral : $\frac{1}{\gamma}\int_{v_{0}}^{0}\frac{1}{(\frac{g}{\gamma}+v^{2})}dv=-\int_{0}^{t}dt$ Recognizing the integral as the standard form $\frac{1}{x^{2}+a^{2}}=\frac{1}{a}tan^{-1}(\frac{x}{a})$ , we write the integral in terms of the arctangent function. This gives us : $\frac{1}{\gamma}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{\frac{g}{\gamma}}})[tan^{-1}(\frac{v}{\sqrt{\frac{g}{\gamma}}})]_{v_{0}}^{0}=-t$ Evaluating the integral at the bounds gives us : $\frac{1}{\sqrt{\gamma g}}tan^{-1}(\frac{\sqrt{\gamma}v_{0}}{\sqrt{g}})=t$ Therefore, the time taken by the ball to rise to its zenith, considering the drag force, is given by $t=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\gamma g}}tan^{-1}(\sqrt{\frac{\gamma}{g}}V_{0})$

Given, drag force, $F=m\gamma v^{2}$ ......(i)

As we know, general equation of force

$a=\gamma v^{2}$

The net retardation of the ball when thrown vertically upward is therefore

$a_{\text{net}}=-(g+\gamma v^{2})=\frac{dv}{dt}$ , where $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity.

Rearranging terms gives us :

$\frac{dv}{g+\gamma v^{2}}=-dt$

We now need to integrate both sides of this equation.

When the ball is thrown upward with velocity $v_{0}$ and reaches its zenith ( "zenith" refers to the highest point that the ball reaches in its upward trajectory.), the velocity is $0$ . The time to reach the zenith is $t$ .

So the integral equation is :

$\int_{v_{0}}^{0}\frac{dv}{\gamma v^{2}+g}=-\int_{0}^{t}dt$

Separating the constants from the integral :

$\frac{1}{\gamma}\int_{v_{0}}^{0}\frac{1}{(\frac{g}{\gamma}+v^{2})}dv=-\int_{0}^{t}dt$

Recognizing the integral as the standard form $\frac{1}{x^{2}+a^{2}}=\frac{1}{a}tan^{-1}(\frac{x}{a})$ , we write the integral in terms of the arctangent function.

This gives us :

$\frac{1}{\gamma}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{\frac{g}{\gamma}}})[tan^{-1}(\frac{v}{\sqrt{\frac{g}{\gamma}}})]_{v_{0}}^{0}=-t$

Evaluating the integral at the bounds gives us :

$\frac{1}{\sqrt{\gamma g}}tan^{-1}(\frac{\sqrt{\gamma}v_{0}}{\sqrt{g}})=t$

Therefore, the time taken by the ball to rise to its zenith, considering the drag force, is given by

$t=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\gamma g}}tan^{-1}(\sqrt{\frac{\gamma}{g}}V_{0})$
